beats.purpose: An Egyptian official purchased Joseph after his sale; following an accusation, his master imprisoned him. Genesis 39:20–21 then records God's continuing presence with Joseph. This is a short causal bridge, not a featured Potiphar episode.

beats.scene: Joseph raised to authority
beats.editorialReason: Pharaoh's approval at 41:37 called the counsel good without any counsel in the selected verses. Restore Joseph's interpretation of seven years of plenty and famine and his recommendation to store grain (41:25–30,33–36).

beats.editorialReason: Keep the previously restored pursuit (14:5–10), Moses's reassurance (14:13–14), the sea crossing (14:15–22) AND the Egyptians' entry into the sea (14:23) before the waters return (14:26–31); removing 14:23 breaks causal continuity.

beats.scene: David anointed by Samuel
beats.editorialReason: Without verses 4–9 the Lord's instruction to Jesse and Samuel's examination of the elder sons are missing before verse 10. Preserve the complete chosen-king episode, replacing the earlier provisional 1Samuel 16:1–3 source bridge.

beats.label: Saul dies and kingship changes
beats.explanation: Saul died in battle against the Philistines, and David subsequently began his reign over Judah at Hebron (1 Samuel 31; 2 Samuel 2:1–4).

beats.scene: David receives the kingdom
Jerusalem becomes David's capital
The Ark brought to Jerusalem
God promises David an enduring royal house
beats.editorialReason: The divine answer in 7:8 begins mid-command to Nathan; verses 1–7 establish David's desire to build God a house and God's response before the covenant promise of an enduring royal dynasty.

movements.title: The Temple and the divided kingdom
movements.purpose: The moral frailty of kings, Temple worship, Solomon's infidelity and division after him

beats.label: David's sin with Bathsheba and Uriah
beats.explanation: David sinned grievously against Bathsheba and Uriah. Nathan confronted him, and David acknowledged his sin before the Lord (2 Samuel 11–12).

beats.scene: Solomon builds the Temple
beats.editorialReason: Preserve the Temple-construction event but omit numerical dimensions from this introductory narrative unit; the Temple's consecration is already narrated in the next original passage.

beats.scene: The Ark enters the dedicated Temple

beats.label: Solomon turns to other gods
beats.explanation: Solomon subsequently turned to foreign gods, and the Lord announced that the kingdom would be torn apart after him, though a portion would remain for David's sake (1 Kings 11:1–13).

beats.scene: The kingdom is foretold to divide
Israel and Judah divide
beats.editorialReason: The final verse 12:24 begins in the middle of Shemaiah's unintroduced quotation. The division is already completed and explained in 12:13–20; do not feature an orphan quotation.

movements.title: Prophetic warning and Israel's judgment
movements.purpose: Idolatry and prophetic calls to fidelity frame Isaiah's distinct messianic oracles; the northern kingdom's fall is a historical event, not a simultaneous fulfillment of every oracle.

beats.label: Elijah confronts Baal's prophets
beats.explanation: Elijah opposed the worship of Baal during Israel's apostasy (1 Kings 18). The following oracles of Isaiah are distinct prophetic witnesses to God's promises, not episodes occurring in one continuous scene (Isaiah 7; 9; 11; 52–53).

beats.scene: The sign of Emmanuel
The promised royal child
The shoot from Jesse
The suffering servant
The northern kingdom falls under judgment
beats.editorialReason: Samaria's fall had an unnamed assailant and should begin by identifying Shalmaneser in 2 Kings 17:3–4; verses 9–12 are omitted because 17:13–18 already interprets Israel's apostasy. This is a shorter overall source passage with a small but necessary pre-original antecedent.

beats.editorialReason: Ezra 6:13 depends on Darius's otherwise absent administrative instructions and named officials; begin with the elders' actual rebuilding and preserve the Temple dedication and Passover.

beats.explanation: After the return, Ezra publicly proclaimed the Law and the community renewed its worship of the Lord (Nehemiah 8:1–8).

beats.label: Maccabean resistance to imposed idolatry
beats.explanation: In later generations, foreign rulers pressured the Jewish people to forsake their law. Mattathias resisted enforced idolatry, beginning the Maccabean struggle (1 Maccabees 2:15–28).

beats.label: Martyrdom and hope of resurrection
beats.explanation: The martyrs under persecution witnessed to Israel's hope in the resurrection, even in the face of death (2 Maccabees 7).
